\section[\ml{രാത്രി}]{\ml{രാത്രി} (rāthri) — night, already hiding inside midnight}

\label{lesson:ML-C24-rathri}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{Warm-up.} {[}PAUSE 2s{]} Last lesson's \emph{divasam} had three words doing three honest jobs. This word's family is smaller, but the split is just as real — and one piece of it, you've technically already heard.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know}
\textbf{\ml{രാത്രി}} (\textbf{rāthri}) — "\textbf{night}" — is a Sanskrit \textbf{tatsama}. You've likely already met a piece of it: \textbf{\ml{പാതിരാ}} (\emph{pāthirā}, "midnight," Chapter 17) is built from \textbf{\ml{പാതി}} (\emph{pāthi}, "half") fused with what's most plausibly a \textbf{shortened form} of this very word — "\textbf{rā}" standing in for the whole of \emph{rāthri} (Chapter 17 itself didn't spell out which word was being shortened, but the parallel Tamil compound, \emph{pāti-y-irāttiri}, points the same way). This lesson gives it its own, full standing.

\begin{culture}
Here's the honest echo from earlier in this arc: just like Hindi's own \textbf{\dv{रात}} (\emph{raat}, ultimately from the same Sanskrit \textbf{\dv{रात्रि}}), Malayalam's \emph{rāthri} traces to \textbf{Proto-Indo-European} \emph{\textbf{*h\textsubscript{1}reh\textsubscript{1}-}} ("\textbf{to rest}") — a \textbf{completely different} PIE root from Latin's \emph{nox} (\emph{\textbf{*nók\textsuperscript{w}ts}}). Two Indo-European languages, two words for "night," that \textbf{look} like they might be old cousins — but genuinely \textbf{aren't}. Same false-cognate story, now confirmed across a second Indo-Aryan-rooted borrowing.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Guided Practice}
{[}PAUSE 1s{]}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item {[}YOU SAY: "rāthri" — "night," already hiding, shortened, inside pāthirā{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: the honest PIE echo — \emph{h\textsubscript{1}reh\textsubscript{1}-, "to rest," like Hindi's raat, NOT related to Latin's nox{]}}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Wrap-up recall}]
{[}PAUSE 3s{]} Where did you already, technically, meet a piece of \textbf{\ml{രാത്രി}} before this lesson? (Shortened to "\textbf{rā}" inside \textbf{\ml{പാതിരാ}}, \emph{pāthirā}, "midnight," Chapter 17.) Does \emph{rāthri}'s PIE root match Latin \emph{nox}'s? (\textbf{No} — \emph{\textbf{*h\textsubscript{1}reh\textsubscript{1}-}} "to rest," a completely different root, the same false-cognate pattern already seen with Hindi's \emph{raat}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\ml{ഇരവ്} / \ml{ഇരുൾ}]{\ml{ഇരവ്} / \ml{ഇരുൾ} — two native words, two jobs}

\label{lesson:ML-C24-native-night-words}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{Warm-up.} {[}PAUSE 2s{]} \textbf{\ml{രാത്രി}} is the ordinary Sanskrit night-word. Malayalam also kept two native Dravidian words, but they do not compete with it in the same way.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ml{ഇരവ്}} (\emph{iravŭ}) is cognate with Tamil \textbf{\ta{இரவு}} (\emph{iravu}) and is traced by one source to Proto-Dravidian \emph{\textbf{*cira}}, “darkness.” It survives mainly as a \textbf{literary or classical-register} synonym for “night.” Poetry is a more likely home for it than everyday conversation.
  \item \textbf{\ml{ഇരുൾ}} (\emph{iruḷ}) descends from Proto-Dravidian \emph{\textbf{*cirVḷ}} and belongs to the pan-Dravidian family Kannada \textbf{\ka{ಇರುಳು}}, Tamil \textbf{\ta{இருள்}}, and Telugu \textbf{\te{ఇరులు}}. It remains current in modern Malayalam—a 2021 film is titled \emph{Irul}—but its ordinary sense is \textbf{darkness}, not night as a time period.
\end{itemize}

This is not one native night-word simply pushed into archaism. It is two native words carrying different pieces of \textbf{\ml{രാത്രി}}’s semantic space: one formal and poetic, the other common but narrower.

\subsection*{Guided Practice}
{[}PAUSE 1s{]}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item {[}YOU SAY: \emph{iravŭ} — literary night{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: \emph{iruḷ} — current darkness{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: related ideas, different modern jobs{]}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Wrap-up recall}]
{[}PAUSE 3s{]} Are \textbf{\ml{ഇരവ്}} and \textbf{\ml{ഇരുൾ}} interchangeable everyday words for night? (\textbf{No.}) Which is literary “night”? (\textbf{iravŭ}.) Which is current “darkness”? (\textbf{iruḷ}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
